cases.label: What must happen soon: the appointed time is near
cases.later: Seven churches in Roman Asia; successive centuries of Christian expectations
cases.kind: Explicit imminent apocalyptic framing with disputed referent and time horizon
cases.original: Greek ἐν τάχει (en tachei, 'soon/quickly', Rev 1:1; 22:6), ἐγγύς (engys, 'near', 1:3; 22:10), and ἔρχομαι ταχύ ('I am coming soon/quickly', 22:7, 12, 20).
cases.setting: The book introduces itself as a revelation addressed to seven churches in the Roman province of Asia. Its prologue and epilogue frame visions of imperial evil, judgment and new creation with repeated imminence language. The book's final form is commonly placed near Domitian's late-first-century reign, though early Nero-era dating and redaction models remain disputed.
cases.laterUse: Christians have applied the passages to first-century divine judgment on Rome or Jerusalem, the quickly unfolding consequences of Christ's resurrection, the end-of-age return still awaited, or the claim that events happen rapidly once initiated. Readings that postpone the promised culmination indefinitely must explain both ἐν τάχει and ἐγγύς and the addressees' context.
cases.relationship: A claim about soon/near events, stated to the author's contemporary readers, intersects the entire vision but does not itself specify a calendar date. 'Swiftly when it happens' can be argued for ταχύ in certain contexts, but it does not automatically cancel the explicitly spatial-temporal 'near' at both bookends. Apocalyptic symbols and stages can carry multiple referents; specify which events have occurred before rating fulfillment.
cases.evidence: The original Greek expressions and named Asian congregations are directly ascertainable. No independently observed end of death, new creation, or universal visible return is documented within that audience's lifespan. Claims that the language refers only to contemporary Roman tribulation, rather than the book's cosmic end, remain interpretive positions that require argument.
cases.sourceStatus: Near-time Greek and original audience explicit; scope and literal fulfillment of complete visions disputed
refs: USCCB critical Introduction to Revelation, authorship and dating

cases.label: The beast, coercive worship and 666/616
cases.later: First-century Roman imperial institutions and subsequent end-time beast interpretations
cases.kind: Apocalyptic political symbol and cryptographic number with significant textual variant
cases.original: Rev 13:18 Greek ψήφισάτω τὸν ἀριθμὸν τοῦ θηρίου ('let them calculate the beast's number'); principal number ἑξακόσιοι ἑξήκοντα ἕξ (666), with ancient 616 variant.
cases.setting: Revelation's sea beast borrows features from Daniel 7's four political beasts, while a land beast promotes worship of the first. In a Roman-Asia setting, imperial authority, emperor worship and restrictions on economic activity provide a historically grounded interpretive backdrop. The seven heads can be associated with Rome's rulers/hills, but the details are not straightforward chronological data.
cases.laterUse: A major scholarly identification reads 666 as 'Neron Caesar' transliterated into Hebrew letters, yielding 666, with a Latinized name spelling yielding 616. Papyrus 115 preserves a form of the 616 variant; it is not a modern numerical invention. Max Nelson (2025) challenges the dominant Nero proposal with a Claudian-house candidate, confirming continuing scholarly disagreement. Many Christian futurist traditions interpret the beast as a still-future political ruler or system.
cases.relationship: The number is a feature of first-century name-number calculation (gematria/isopsephy) and has manuscript variation that must be recorded before modern identifications. The text invokes Danielic empire imagery, not a directly demonstrable future identification from a present-day technology, ID system or political figure. Rome-centered readings are historically contextual but not proof that every apocalyptic image was fulfilled by Nero.
cases.evidence: Roman imperial rule, Nero's death in 68 CE, Asian provincial imperial cults, and textual witnesses to 666/616 are historically documented. The chapter's supernatural miracles, global control and final downfall are not independently verified as an integrated literal event; scholars dispute single-name decoding and the intended audience/dating.
cases.sourceStatus: Roman imperial context and 666/616 variants supported; beast identity and any full predictive fulfillment disputed
refs: Max Nelson (2025), A Concealed Claudian: The Meaning of 666 in Revelation
USCCB Revelation Introduction, first-century Asia/Rome context
Theological Studies scholarly discussion of 616 Papyrus 115 (via Nelson)

cases.label: Thousand-year reign, final judgment and new Jerusalem
cases.later: Jewish restoration imagery, Christian premillennial/amillennial/postmillennial expectations, claimed end of death
cases.kind: Eschatological vision reusing older restoration images; duration and sequence contested
cases.original: Rev 20:2 χίλια ἔτη ('a thousand years'); Rev 21:1 οὐρανὸν καινὸν καὶ γῆν καινήν ('new heaven and new earth'); Rev 21:4 θάνατος οὐκ ἔσται ἔτι ('death will be no more').
cases.setting: A vision following the beast's judgment depicts Satan bound for one thousand years, martyrs reigning, a later release and final battle, judgment of the dead, and a new heaven and new earth descending with a vast cubic Jerusalem. The author reworks Isaiah 25, 65–66, Ezekiel 37–48 and Danielic resurrection/court imagery. The 'new city' has no separate temple because God and the Lamb embody its sanctuary.
cases.laterUse: Premillennialists read a future distinct thousand-year reign followed by final judgment; amillennialists understand the thousand years symbolically as Christ's present reign with a final consummation; postmillennial readings view an extended gospel transformation before final return. Jewish and Christian readings of Isaiah/Ezekiel antecedents differ. Catholic USCCB notes explicitly interpret the millennium as a symbolic, rather than literal, long period.
cases.relationship: The gigantic cube, innumerable architectural jewels and replacement of sun/temple are structured symbols; a blanket assertion that the material describes exactly 1,000 elapsed modern years is a tradition-specific premise. The promise of no more death is a more direct observable end-state condition, and no historical period has fulfilled it as a universal physical fact.
cases.evidence: Earlier intertexts and competing reception histories can be verified. No independently observable global resurrection, permanent ending of death, destruction of the cosmos or descent of a jewel-built heavenly metropolis has been recorded. A future expectation is logically different from an already verified historical event.
cases.sourceStatus: Apocalyptic intertexts and competing millennium interpretations attested; final world transformation unverified

cases.label: Isaiah is named over a three-passage composite quotation
cases.later: Mark 1:2–3, applied to John the Baptist's ministry
cases.kind: Composite literary quotation with 'Isaiah' vs 'prophets' textual variant
cases.original: Mark 1:2 ἐν τῷ Ἠσαΐᾳ τῷ προφήτῃ ('in Isaiah the prophet') in the early critical witnesses; later variant ἐν τοῖς προφήταις ('in the prophets'). Mark's first quoted messenger wording echoes Exodus 23:20 and Malachi 3:1; 1:3 cites Isaiah 40:3.
cases.setting: Exodus's messenger originally guides Israel toward the land; Malachi warns of coming purification and a messenger before YHWH's arrival; Isaiah 40 announces comfort and a wilderness highway for YHWH during exile/restoration. None originally names John the Baptist.
cases.laterUse: Mark makes John the Baptist the preparing wilderness messenger for Jesus and captions both source fragments with Isaiah. Matthew and Luke rework these traditions in their own order. Many manuscripts read 'in the prophets,' a possible smoothing of the difficult naming issue; the older/widely attested critical reading favors Isaiah.
cases.relationship: Mark's introductory quotation is conflated from at least two different prophet texts and language echoed from Exodus. It is not a single uncontested exact forward-looking prediction. Attribution to the leading prophet can be an ancient composition convention; a mistaken attribution or later editorial correction are alternative scholarly explanations, but each must explain the manuscript evidence.
cases.evidence: Direct primary comparison and well-documented textual variants establish the wording change. NET critical notes specify witnesses and explain why the harder Isaiah reading has early support; this determines which 'attribution problem' an analyst is actually judging. The Gospel's literary reuse does not independently corroborate John the Baptist as a uniquely predicted individual.
cases.sourceStatus: Three-source composite and early Isaiah attribution supported; original referents distinct from later Christian reading
refs: Mark 1:2–3 with footnotes and texts of Exodus/Malachi/Isaiah
NET critical apparatus on Isaiah vs prophets wording
Monograph on OT quotation adaptation in Mark (2023)

cases.label: Psalm 22's garment-lot lament becomes two fulfillment actions
cases.kind: Poetic lament reused as a passion scene with narrative elaboration
cases.original: Psalm 22:18 יְחַלְּקוּ בְגָדַי לָהֶם וְעַל־לְבוּשִׁי יַפִּילוּ גוֹרָל ('they divide my clothes among themselves, and cast lots for my clothing').
cases.setting: Psalm 22 is a first-person lament by a speaker who believes he has been abandoned and exposed to humiliating violence, before a turn toward divine deliverance and praise. Its two garment expressions use synonymous poetic parallelism to depict enemies treating the sufferer as doomed; no first-century Roman soldiers are named.
cases.laterUse: All four canonical passion accounts mention garments and casting lots. John alone quotes Psalm 22 directly at this exact point and distinguishes the soldiers' dividing several garments from separately casting lots for a seamless tunic; the USCCB note describes the scene as a literal division of poetic parallelism into two narrated actions.
cases.relationship: The earlier lyric describes humiliation and dispossession within a prayer, while the Gospel treats it as Jesus' fulfilled scripture. Multiple Gospels may preserve shared tradition and cannot automatically be counted as four independent eyewitness confirmations; deliberate narrative shaping around scripture is a live historical-critical possibility.
cases.evidence: Psalm wording and John's allocation of the two actions can be compared. There is no external material record of the soldiers' precise lottery, so the evangelist's assertion of fulfillment cannot independently establish that every physical detail occurred as narrated.
cases.sourceStatus: Scriptural quotation and parallelism clear; specific allocation scene lacks independent attestation
refs: USCCB John 19:23–24 and note contrasting John and Synoptics

cases.label: The Ethiopian official asks who Isaiah's suffering servant is
cases.kind: Ancient Greek servant quotation used as a Christian teaching interpretation
cases.original: Acts 8:33 quotes Greek ἐν τῇ ταπεινώσει ἡ κρίσις αὐτοῦ ἤρθη ('in his humiliation his justice/judgment was taken away'); Hebrew Isaiah 53:8 reads מֵעֹצֶר וּמִמִּשְׁפָּט לֻקָּח ('by/from oppression and judgment he was taken').
cases.setting: Isaiah's servant poem appears in Isaiah 52:13–53:12 and has disputed identity, including collective Israel, representative individual and other proposals; Isaiah 49:3 can call the servant Israel even as 49:5 depicts a mission to restore Israel. The Hebrew and ancient Greek forms of 53:8 differ significantly in their portrayal of oppression and judgment.
cases.laterUse: Acts narrates a royal official of a Nubian queen returning from worship in Jerusalem while reading Isaiah's Greek form. He asks Philip whom the prophet means, and Philip teaches that Jesus is the referent, after which the official is baptized. The narrative's question records that the passage's identity was not treated as self-evident.
cases.relationship: Acts quotes the old Greek more closely than the Hebrew on the 'humiliation/justice' clause and applies an earlier servant poem to Jesus. The later interpretation is clearly documented as a claim by Acts' author and characters; it does not independently establish the earlier writer's intended identity or the historicity of the encounter.
cases.evidence: USCCB's critical Acts 8 note identifies the quoted verses and evangelization role, and a direct comparison shows Hebrew/Greek wording differences. The reported angelic instructions, sudden disappearance and precise dialogue are only attested within Acts, not confirmed by independent contemporary records.
cases.sourceStatus: Greek quotation and Jesus application explicit; Hebrew/Greek differences and earlier servant identity remain contested
refs: Commentary comparing Hebrew Isaiah 53:8 and Acts' LXX wording
